issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings based on documents do not become errors of law unless the documents were misconstrued.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court both found that the deity and the properties were subject to a public religious and charitable endowment.
The appeal challenged the legal inference drawn from numerous documents, but the Supreme Court found no misconstruction of the documents produced.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent findings were factual findings and were not shown to be legally erroneous; the appeal disclosed no misconstruction warranting their reversal.
issues.legal_principle: An inference drawn from documents is a finding of fact where the documents have not been misconstrued. A mistaken inference is not, for that reason alone, a finding of law.

predicates.civil_appeal_against_concurrent_findings: A party appealed a decision in which the lower courts reached the same factual finding.
predicates.findings_rest_on_documents: The lower courts based their finding on documentary evidence.
predicates.no_document_misconstrued: The appellate court found no misconstruction of the documents on which the finding rested.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal challenges concurrent findings based on documents, and no document was misconstrued, the concurrent factual finding stands.

issues.legal_issue: Admissions by a claimant or predecessors in title, supported by official property records, require cogent rebuttal before a contrary claim can succeed.
material_facts: The appellant and predecessors in title repeatedly acknowledged that the properties belonged to the deity or its institution and that the family members managed them rather than owned them.
The Inam Commissioner recorded the relevant village grants as permanent religious endowments after a predecessor challenged their classification as personal grants.
Revenue records likewise described the grants as religious endowments.

The appellant did not produce the original grant documents referred to in the records and history of the institution, and the courts found that the evidence did not displace the admissions and official records.
issues.conclusion: The admissions and revenue records supported the finding that the properties were endowment property; the appellant did not rebut them with cogent and convincing evidence.
issues.legal_principle: An admission is the best evidence an opposing party can rely on and, though not conclusive, is decisive unless successfully withdrawn or shown to be erroneous. The Judicial Committee in Arunachellam Chetty v. Venkatachellapathi Guru Swamigal (1919) treated Inam Register information as highly important where better evidence was unavailable. In Srinivasa Chariar v. Evalappa Mudaliar (1922), it held that where property is shown by its discoverable origins to be trust property, the trustee bears a heavy onus to establish a personal acquisition by clear and unimpeachable evidence. The court also distinguished Babu Bhagwan Din v. Gir Har Saroop (1939), where the grant was made to an individual and heirs and there was no contrary evidence.

rule.if: proceeding_to_determine_public_trust_status and prior_owners_admitted_endowment_ownership and official_records_support_endowment and claimant_failed_to_rebut_admissions

predicates.proceeding_to_determine_public_trust_sta: The proceeding seeks to determine whether property is privately owned or held as a public religious or charitable endowment.
predicates.prior_owners_admitted_endowment_ownershi: The claimant or predecessors in title acknowledged that the property belonged to the religious institution rather than to them personally.
predicates.official_records_support_endowment: Official property records or administrative findings described the property as endowment property.
predicates.claimant_failed_to_rebut_admissions: The claimant did not produce cogent evidence showing that the admissions and official records were erroneous.

issues.definition: In a proceeding about public trust status, prior admissions and supporting official records that the claimant fails to rebut mean that a claim of private ownership is not established.

issues.legal_issue: Long-standing public worship and a separate endowment support an inference that a religious institution is public unless contrary circumstances are established.
material_facts: The public had access to the temple throughout the day, and there was no evidence that worshippers had been excluded from worship as a matter of right.
The public had worshipped there continuously for a long period.
The temple was extensive, had facilities for large gatherings, and hosted public festivals, processions, worship and feeding of visitors.
The deity received grants and endowments for worship and festivals, and the institution's administration and history were consistent with public use.
issues.conclusion: The deity and temple were public, and the evidence established a public right of worship.
issues.legal_principle: Under the definition of a temple in section 9 of the Hindu Religious Endowments Act, as discussed in Narayanan v. Hindu Religious Endowments Board, public character may be inferred from the institution's nature, public use and administration. Once long public worship and a separate endowment for the deity are established, dedication for public use may fairly be inferred unless the contrary is shown. Public offerings alone are not necessarily sufficient, as noted in Babu Bhagwan Din v. Gir Har Saroop; the extent of the temple, endowments and public use are relevant circumstances.

rule.if: proceeding_to_determine_public_or_private_religious_status and long_public_worship and separate_endowment_for_deity and (public_access_without_exclusion or public_scale_and_rituals)

predicates.proceeding_to_determine_public_or_privat: The proceeding asks whether a religious institution is public or private.
predicates.long_public_worship: Members of the public have worshipped at the institution over a long period.
predicates.separate_endowment_for_deity: Property or income has been set apart for the deity or its worship.
predicates.public_access_without_exclusion: The public has been admitted for worship without evidence of exclusion as a matter of right.
predicates.public_scale_and_rituals: The institution's scale, ceremonies or activities indicate use by a worshipping public beyond a private household.

issues.definition: In a proceeding about religious status, long public worship and a separate endowment, together with public access or public-scale activities, mean that the institution is public.

issues.legal_issue: Temporary movement of an idol for worship does not by itself establish that the idol or temple is private.
material_facts: The deity was temporarily taken out for processions, visits and worship at other locations and was returned to its established temple.
A substitute idol remained at the temple during the deity's absence.
The temporary movements had continued for generations with the consent of the worshipping public, and large numbers of worshippers followed the deity.
issues.conclusion: The temporary movement of the deity did not make the temple private or the deity a family idol.
issues.legal_principle: The court considered Ram Soondur Thakoor v. Taruck Chunder Turkoruttun (1873), Hari Raghunath v. Anantji Bhikaji (1920), Pramatha Nath Mullick v. Pradyumna Kumar Mullick (1925), and Venkatachala v. Sambasiva (1927). These authorities distinguish temporary movement, or movement with the worshippers' consent, from permanent removal that would effectively establish a different temple. The court found no authority or text establishing that an idol installed in a movable form cannot be moved temporarily for worship.

rule.if: dispute_over_public_or_private_temple and idol_moved_temporarily_for_worship and idol_returned_to_temple and (substitute_remained_at_temple or worshippers_consented)

predicates.dispute_over_public_or_private_temple: The proceeding disputes whether a temple or deity is public or private.
predicates.idol_moved_temporarily_for_worship: Those managing the temple temporarily moved the idol to facilitate worship, processions or visits.
predicates.idol_returned_to_temple: The idol was returned to its established temple after the temporary movement.
predicates.substitute_remained_at_temple: A substitute idol remained at the temple while the principal idol was away.
predicates.worshippers_consented: The temporary movement occurred with the consent of the worshipping public.

issues.definition: When an idol is moved temporarily for worship and returned to its temple, with a substitute remaining there or with worshippers' consent, that movement does not establish private status.

issues.legal_issue: A declaration affecting a deity's property cannot effectively bind the deity when the deity is not joined as a party.
material_facts: The appellant sought a declaration that the properties were privately owned, including properties for which the High Court had expressed a view that they might be private.
The deity was not joined as a party, although the trial court had warned that the suit might fail if the deity proved to be necessary.
The appellant opposed the request to join the deity and sought to rely instead on representation of the Hindu public under the civil procedure rule for representative suits.
The appellant had not distinguished the various properties in his ownership claim and sought to join the deity only at a late stage of the appeal.
issues.conclusion: No declaration of private ownership could be granted in respect of the properties where the deity was not a party; representation of the Hindu community did not bind the deity.
issues.legal_principle: In a suit seeking a declaration affecting the deity's interests, the deity is a necessary party for an effective and binding decision; a representative suit for the Hindu community does not itself bind the deity. The court referred to Order 1, rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure and distinguished the late-stage course adopted in Pramatha Nath Mullick v. Pradyumna Kumar Mullick (1925) and Kanhaiya Lal v. Hamid Ali (1933), given the claimant's opposition to joinder and the trial court's warning.

rule.if: declaratory_suit_affecting_deity_property and deity_not_joined and (claimant_opposed_deity_joinder or deity_not_independently_represented)

predicates.declaratory_suit_affecting_deity_propert: The suit seeks a declaration about ownership of property that may belong to a deity or its religious institution.
predicates.deity_not_joined: The deity was not made a party to the suit.
predicates.claimant_opposed_deity_joinder: The claimant resisted a request to make the deity a party.
predicates.deity_not_independently_represented: No independent representative appeared in the proceeding to protect the deity's interests.

issues.definition: In a suit for a declaration affecting deity property, if the deity is not joined and its interests are not independently represented or the claimant opposed joinder, the declaration of private ownership is refused.

issues.legal_issue: A suit limited to determining public trust status should not decide collateral individual rights in the property.
material_facts: The suit was brought to determine whether the deity and properties were subject to a public religious and charitable trust.
The trial court also made findings about the customary worship, maintenance and emoluments of individual defendants.
Those individual rights were asserted in response to the appellant's claim that he held all rights in the properties.
issues.conclusion: The courts below should have refrained from deciding the individual defendants' rights because those matters were not necessary to determine the public character of the trust; the Supreme Court gave no further direction on them.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(3) of the Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920, framed the suit as one for determining the relevant trust status. The court stated that other matters concerning individuals' rights should not be decided in a suit of that character, while declining to give a direction because the suit as a whole had been dismissed.

predicates.proceeding_limited_to_public_trust_statu: The proceeding is confined to deciding whether property is held in a public religious or charitable trust.
predicates.individual_rights_are_collateral_to_stat: The claimed rights of particular individuals are not necessary to determine whether the trust is public.

issues.definition: When a proceeding is limited to public trust status and individual rights are collateral to that status, those rights are not decided in the status proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A respondent who seeks relief altering a costs order on appeal must challenge that order by cross-objection.
material_facts: The trial court had awarded two sets of costs, and the High Court modified the order to allow only one set.
Respondents sought further relief concerning the costs order in the Supreme Court but had not filed cross-objections to the High Court's decision.
issues.conclusion: No further relief concerning costs could be granted to those respondents because they had not cross-objected to the High Court's order.
issues.legal_principle: A respondent seeking relief against an order made by the court below must challenge that order by cross-objection; absent such an objection, the appellate court granted no relief on costs.

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter is an appeal in a civil proceeding.
predicates.respondent_seeks_change_to_costs_order: A respondent asks the appellate court to alter a costs order made below.
predicates.no_cross_objection: The respondent did not file a cross-objection challenging that order.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, a respondent seeking a change to a costs order without filing a cross-objection is denied that relief.
